planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; give CranRazz room to reach full size, since it grows as vigorously as older large-form butterfly bush cultivars.

directions: CranRazz bears long, dense flower spikes up to 8 inches, colored a vivid cranberry-red distinct from the more common magenta and purple butterfly bush shades. It blooms in repeated flushes from summer until frost on a vigorous, well-branched, upright shrub, and the fragrant spikes work well in cut arrangements as well as in the garden. Like other full-size Buddleja davidii hybrids it is a strong butterfly and hummingbird attractant, and it benefits from a hard cutback to a low framework in late winter since it flowers on new wood.

common_name: Peacock Butterfly Bush (English Butterfly Series Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Peacock keeps a compact frame roughly a third the size of standard Buddleja davidii, suiting smaller beds.

directions: Peacock is part of the English Butterfly series bred in England by Elizabeth Keep to combine full-size flower quality with a compact, densely branched habit. Its pink flower panicles are the largest in the series, often reaching 12 to 14 inches long, held on a shrub that stays noticeably smaller than classic large-form Buddleja davidii cultivars. It flowers from summer into early autumn and draws heavy butterfly and hummingbird activity, and an annual hard cutback in late winter keeps its compact scale and flowering vigor intact.

common_name: Purple Emperor Butterfly Bush (English Butterfly Series Deep Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; its compact English Butterfly series habit fits smaller borders and large containers.

directions: Purple Emperor produces masses of deep purple flower spikes on a compact, upright shrub bred by Elizabeth Keep as part of the English Butterfly series, which was developed to shrink classic Buddleja davidii size without sacrificing bloom density. It flowers heavily from midsummer into fall and is a strong draw for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. Cut the plant back hard in late winter, since flowers form on new growth and the annual renewal keeps the compact form from becoming leggy.

common_name: Adonis Blue Butterfly Bush (English Butterfly Series Deep Violet-Blue Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; expect an arching, compact frame to about 5 feet, smaller than classic Buddleja davidii selections.

directions: Adonis Blue, another English Butterfly series introduction bred by Elizabeth Keep, carries fragrant flower panicles up to 8 inches long in an unusually deep, dusky blue-violet rather than the paler lavender-blue of many older cultivars. Blooming from summer into early autumn on an arching, compact shrub, it is a consistent draw for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Give it a hard cutback in late winter to renew the wood that carries the coming season's flowers.

common_name: Wisteria Lane Butterfly Bush (Weeping Pale Lilac Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; its pendent flower clusters are shown off best where the plant can be viewed from below, such as atop a low wall or slope.

directions: Wisteria Lane, bred by Hans Hansen of Walters Gardens, is named for its long, dense, pendent panicles of fragrant pale lilac flowers that hang and drape from the branches in a manner reminiscent of wisteria racemes, an unusual habit among butterfly bush cultivars that typically hold flowers upright. The compact, bushy shrub has narrow, woolly, grey-green leaves and blooms from midsummer into autumn. Like other Buddleja davidii selections it draws butterflies and hummingbirds reliably and benefits from a hard late-winter cutback to renew flowering wood.

common_name: Monarch Prince Charming Butterfly Bush (Cerise-Pink Compact Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Prince Charming is bred small but not dwarf, so give it more room than the miniature Buzz or Pugster series.

directions: Prince Charming is part of the Monarch series bred by Hans Hansen of Walters Gardens to be small-statured, well-branched plants without going as dwarf as some other modern series. It carries bright cerise-pink flower spikes roughly 10 inches long from summer into fall on a tidy, well-proportioned shrub. It attracts butterflies and hummingbirds readily and, like other Buddleja davidii cultivars, should be cut back hard in late winter to renew the flowering wood.

common_name: Monarch Crown Jewels Butterfly Bush (Gold-Leaved Magenta-Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; distinct from the unrelated existing Crown Jewels hardy hibiscus and Crown Jewels ternstroemia, this is a gold-foliaged Buddleja shrub.

directions: Crown Jewels, part of the Monarch series from Walters Gardens, stands out among butterfly bush cultivars for its gold to chartreuse foliage, which provides season-long color even before the magenta-purple, upward-pointing flower spikes open in summer. The contrast between bright foliage and rich flower color makes it a distinctive accent shrub rather than a purely background plant. It attracts butterflies and hummingbirds like other Buddleja and should be cut back hard in late winter to keep the plant compact and well-flowered.

common_name: Flutterby Petite Tutti Frutti Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Raspberry-Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; its 2 to 2.5 foot dwarf size suits containers and small beds where full-size butterfly bush would overwhelm the space.

directions: Flutterby Petite Tutti Frutti is one of the dwarf, sterile-to-near-sterile Buddleja developed through the Podaras breeding program at Cornell University and marketed by Ball Horticultural, bred to combine a uniformly compact 2 to 2.5 foot habit with continuous summer-to-frost bloom. Its raspberry-pink flower spikes are held densely over the small, upright mound of foliage. Because the series sets very little seed, it poses much less self-seeding risk than older Buddleja davidii cultivars while still drawing butterflies and hummingbirds readily.

common_name: Flutterby Petite Snow White Butterfly Bush (Dwarf White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; pair with the other Flutterby Petite colors for a compact mixed-color butterfly bush planting.

directions: Snow White is the white-flowered member of the dwarf Flutterby Petite series bred through the Podaras program at Cornell University, staying in the 2 to 2.5 foot range in both height and width. Its clean white flower spikes bloom continuously from summer through frost against a dense, compact mound of foliage, and the series' low seed set means far less self-sowing than full-size Buddleja davidii. It remains a strong pollinator plant for butterflies and hummingbirds despite its small footprint, making it well suited to containers and small borders.

common_name: White Ball Butterfly Bush (Classic Compact White-Flowered Buddleja Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; this older cultivar has proven garden performance dating back decades.

directions: White Ball is a long-established Buddleja hybrid, released in Boskoop, the Netherlands, in 1974, valued for its compact, rounded habit and dense clusters of pure white flowers. It predates the modern wave of dwarf, sterile-bred series but still offers a smaller, tidier footprint than large classic Buddleja davidii cultivars like White Profusion. It flowers over a long summer-to-fall season and draws butterflies and hummingbirds consistently, benefiting from an annual hard cutback in late winter to keep its rounded form dense.
